fixes.explanation: Envy is the one, friend. David says, "Do not fret over those who do evil; do not envy those who do wrong." Those are two separate warnings, and he closes the door on both. Fretting and envying will eat up your whole afternoon, and I speak from experience.

Peace is what we all want, but David says the opposite. He says, "Refrain from anger and abandon wrath; do not fret—it can only bring harm." So the fretting doesn't lead to peace. David wants you to put it down.

Justice does show up in this psalm, but not here. David says, "Refrain from anger and abandon wrath; do not fret—it can only bring harm." The harm is what he says fretting brings, not justice. Elsewhere, he says the LORD will bring forth your justice like the noonday sun (Psalm 37:6).

True. David says, "Better is the little of the righteous than the abundance of many who are wicked." A little in the hands of the righteous beats the abundance of many who are wicked. David has done the math and he's not worried.

Forever, friend. David says, "The LORD knows the days of the blameless, and their inheritance will last forever." He knows every one of their days, and the inheritance outlasts them all. Forever is a long time, even for a baker with a full oven.

Iron sounds tough, and tough things sound like they last. But David doesn't pick iron. He says, "They will vanish; like smoke they will fade away." The picture is smoke, something you watch fade until it's gone.

Rulers would be a big job for the children, but David doesn't say it. He says, "They are ever generous and quick to lend, and their children are a blessing." The word is blessing. Rulers aren't in the verse.

Leaving the land isn't what David says about them. He says, "They are ever generous and quick to lend, and their children are a blessing." The word he gives for the children is blessing. The land isn't mentioned in this verse.

Strength is a fair guess, since the LORD is strong. But David names something else here. He says, "For the LORD loves justice and will not forsake His saints." Strength never comes up in the verse, and what the LORD loves is justice, friend.

Riddles would make a fun dinner guest. But David says the righteous man's mouth "utters wisdom, and his tongue speaks justice." Wisdom and justice are the two things he names. No riddles in the verse.

It's true, friend, and I'd bet that one tripped you up. David says, "The law of his God is in his heart; his steps do not falter." The law is in the heart of the righteous man. Don't let a True or False card talk you out of it.

That's it. David says, "I have seen a wicked, ruthless man flourishing like a well-rooted native tree, yet he passed away and was no more; though I searched, he could not be found." The man was flourishing, and then he was gone. David even says he searched, and the man could not be found.

David does say the man was flourishing like a well-rooted native tree, friend. But the next verse turns it around: "…yet he passed away and was no more…" So he didn't keep on growing richer. He passed away, and David searched and could not find him.

Judge is a fair guess, but it's not the word David picks here. He says, "The salvation of the righteous is from the LORD; He is their stronghold in time of trouble." A stronghold is somewhere you run when trouble comes, and that's what David calls the LORD for them. Run to Him, friend.
Offerings are a fair guess, but they aren't the reason in this verse. David says the LORD rescues and saves them "…because they take refuge in Him." The reason is where they run when trouble comes.
